extracted.intended_audience: actors, improvisation teachers, theater educators, students, and general readers interested in theater history and pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and practical criteria for creating and teaching theater games and improvisation methods that develop actors' spontaneity, ensemble skills, and accessibility across cultures and ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game focus / problem-based exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Each game or exercise has a focus, a problem to be solved by the players as a group, so that lessons are learned through play (experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design games with a clear group problem or focus so participants discover theatrical rules organically; use the game’s constraint as the teaching point rather than explicit lecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in universal improv ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone can act. Everyone can improvise. Anyone who wishes to can play in the theater and learn to become stageworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach assuming students can develop skills regardless of perceived talent; avoid excluding learners on the basis of 'talent' or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning through experience (non-directive learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: We learn through experience and experiencing, and no one teaches anyone anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experiential exercises over didactic instruction—facilitate situations where students learn by doing and reflecting rather than receiving top-down explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present-time attention and intuition activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Through focused attention, a player can be in the present time, their intuition activated and their whole body alert and ready to play—physical states that benefit theatrical communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use games that cultivate presence, bodily awareness, and quick attentional shifts to improve spontaneity and communication on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of space objects instead of props/sets
rubrics_metrics.description: In theater games, space objects replace props and sets, which opens the possibility for theatrical transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage imagination and physicalization by having participants treat empty space or imagined objects as concrete elements; this trains flexibility and transformation skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation as core improvisational goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin called transformation the heart of improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises should aim to produce moments of transformation—shifts in relationship, status, or environment—so players practice creating theatrical change out of simple material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-authoritarian, non-verbal, non-psychological teaching methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Her teaching methods [are] non-authoritarian, non-verbal, and non-psychological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hierarchical, lecture-based, or clinical-interpretive approaches; favor facilitator prompts, games, and embodied practice rather than verbal analysis or psychological labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-based, non-judgmental evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Her evaluation methods instead involve the whole group in a non-judgmental process that lets students learn for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use peer and ensemble feedback processes that refrain from shaming or approval/disapproval dynamics; create a supportive group context for learning and risk-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and linguistic accessibility through play
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures about traditional theater techniques were useless with children or adults with limited English skills, but when those lessons became the focus of a game, the students were able to incorporate them organically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ movement, games, and non-verbal activities to teach across language and cultural barriers; design exercises that communicate theatrical concepts without heavy verbal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative problem-solving via game creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The games emerged out of necessity. I didn’t sit at home and dream them up. When I had a problem (directing) I made up a game. Then another problem came up, I just made up a new game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop games responsively to address concrete directing or ensemble problems; iterate and invent exercises tailored to the group’s needs rather than using one-size-fits-all drills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play and non-competitive structure develop social skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Play involves social values... The spirit of play develops social adaptability, ethics, mental and emotional control, and imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor non-competitive games to teach cooperation, rule-negotiation, socialization, language skills, and moral reasoning; emphasize agreed rules and shared responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-as-player and improvised performance practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the first modern improvisational theater performances emerged... with players taking suggestions from the audience to create scene improvisations and plays. Game Theater audience members were invited to join the company playing theater games in performance, a true expression of Spolin’s concept of the audience as fellow player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance contexts, incorporate audience suggestions, invite participation, and use short-form improvisation structures that allow spontaneous scene creation with minimal rehearsal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structured exercises to 'fool' spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercises are artifices against artificiality, structures designed to almost fool spontaneity into being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide formal constraints or prompts that channel spontaneity rather than suppress it—design scaffolds that make genuine improvisation more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theater games as ensemble/rehearsal tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiner: 'After that, these relatively inexperienced actors who hadn’t known each other became a cohesive group.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use games in rehearsal to build group cohesion, chemistry, and ensemble truth quickly; games can substitute for or precede traditional rehearsals to create believable relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad applicability to educational, therapeutic, and community settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin conducted workshops... for public school systems, for drama therapy programs, in mental health facilities and for prisoners; her methods continue to find new practitioners in a wide array of therapeutic applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt game-based methods for diverse institutional contexts (schools, therapy, corrections, community centers) with sensitivity to each population’s needs and objectives.
